remarks: Hiring a consultant for GST filing is optional and depends on the taxpayer's own knowledge of the process and time constraints.

findings.text: GST tax filing is entirely online through the GST portal; physical visits are not required for routine filing.
Taxpayers who lack sufficient knowledge of the GST filing process often hire consultants, resulting in additional compliance costs.
Taxpayers can respond to notices or queries raised by the department entirely through the online portal.
Late filing automatically triggers a calculated late fee; no manual assessment is needed.
Regular and composition taxpayers follow different filing requirements within the same online system.
Step-by-step instructions, user guides with screenshots, and GST-related advisories are available to help taxpayers file independently.
The expert recommended continuing to provide clear, step-by-step guidance to help taxpayers complete filing independently.
The expert recommended simplifying filing instructions to reduce taxpayer dependence on consultants and the associated costs.
The expert recommended promoting awareness of filing due dates, late fees, and interest to help taxpayers avoid delays.
The expert recommended strengthening online support for resolving taxpayer queries and responding to notices.
The 11th of the month was referenced as a filing date during the discussion, though the ED does not detail the full filing calendar by return type.
No statutory fee is charged for filing GST returns.

gaps.text: Only the 11th of the month is referenced as a filing date; the ED does not lay out the complete filing calendar for different return types.
No deemed-approval or automatic-acceptance mechanism is described for GST tax filing.
No specific percentage or figure is given for how many taxpayers use consultants for filing (unlike the GST Registration ED for the same state, which cites approximately 60%).
Entirely online, system-calculated tax liability and automatic late-fee calculation remove manual assessment steps.
Availability of step-by-step guides with screenshots and GST advisories supports independent filing.

timeline.text: The maximum timeline for processing a GST tax refund is 60 days; after processing, the approved amount generally takes an additional 5-7 working days to be credited to the applicant's bank account.

documents: Supporting documents relevant to the type of GST refund being claimed (generally around 3-5 documents, depending on refund category)

deemedApproval.text: No deemed-approval mechanism is specified for GST tax refund.

validity.text: A specific validity period for GST tax refund approval is not specified; the refund is processed based on the application and supporting documents submitted.

fees.text: No statutory fee is charged for GST tax refund applications; the process is entirely online and free of charge.

steps.title: Applicant submits GST tax refund application online
Applicant uploads required supporting documents (approx. 3-5, varies by refund type)
Department examines documents and circulates them to relevant departments for checking

remarks: Taxpayers may use consultants for assistance with refund applications, but hiring one is not mandatory.

findings.text: The GST refund process is entirely online and paperless, from application through document verification to refund order.
The department circulates submitted refund documents to relevant other departments for checking before processing.
Missing or inadequate documentation leads to deficiency notices, additional clarification requests, and rework in the refund process.
After a refund is processed (within the 60-day maximum), the credited amount generally takes an additional 5-7 working days to reach the applicant's bank account.
Applicants can respond to deficiency notices and submit additional documents entirely through the online portal.
No statutory fee or service charge is levied for GST tax refund applications.
The expert recommended providing clear guidance on the documents required for each type of GST tax refund.
The expert recommended ensuring applicants receive clear and specific information about document deficiencies for timely correction.
The expert recommended simplifying the clarification and resubmission process to reduce repeated submissions and rework.
The expert recommended ensuring timely processing of refund applications within the prescribed 60-day timeline.
Using a consultant for refund assistance is optional, not mandatory.
The number of documents required (around 3-5) varies depending on the type of refund claimed.

gaps.text: The specific documents required per refund category (the 'around 3-5 documents') are not itemised — only a general count is given.
No deemed-approval mechanism exists if the 60-day processing timeline is exceeded.
The specific 'relevant departments' the refund application is circulated to for checking are not named.
The entirely paperless refund process, with online deficiency handling and direct bank-account credit, reduces applicant visits.

ed.location: Training Hall, Directorate of Disaster Management(Apada Pravandhak Vibhag), Link Road, Near Anti-corruption Office, Sri Vijayapuram

remarks: The ED's header lists the experts as an Inspector of Factories and a Labour Inspector from the Labour Department, A&N Administration, but the body text describes a municipal water-supply process (E-File, councillor certificates, municipal pipe network, 271 wells) — the stated experts/department do not match the service process described, indicating a likely metadata mismatch in the source document.
The municipal council's water supply is supported by 24 wards, a pipeline distribution network, public wells, and tanker supply; it also receives treated water from APWD.

During periods of low water availability (e.g. when the dam level falls in summer), additional water is supplied via tankers, and the department is developing additional storage infrastructure (Jodanala and Atampad reservoirs).

findings.text: The ED header's listed experts (Inspector of Factories, Labour Inspector, Labour Department) do not match the municipal water-supply process described in the body text, suggesting a metadata/source mismatch.
No fixed departmental timeline for resolving or approving a water-connection application is specified — no Right to Services Act, EODB Act, or Citizen Charter timeline is cited.
The regular water-connection application is processed mainly through the E-File/online system, with very limited hard-copy files.
Approval authority level depends on the connection category/size, with larger connections handled at a higher level.
Water connection charges are flat monthly fees (₹50/month for one connection, ₹60/month for two), not tied to connection size or usage.
Payment can be made online or via swipe, with cash accepted up to ₹2,000.
The main operational burden is reduced water availability in summer when the dam level falls, requiring supplementary tanker supply.
The municipal council uses roughly 271 public wells, including heritage/Japanese wells (some motorised), as a supplementary water source during shortages — considered replicable elsewhere.
Water samples are tested regularly using testing kits, including routine checks and testing triggered by complaints.
Complaints related to water quality or supply are recorded and inspected by the concerned section, with testing carried out where required.
No recommendation specific to the application/approval process was stated; the discussion focused mainly on water availability and supply infrastructure.
No risk-based classification system for water connections was identified during the discussion.

gaps.text: The document's header identifies the experts as 'Ajay Kumar, Inspector of Factories' and 'Prathush Narayan, Labour Inspector,' from the 'Labour Department, A&N Administration,' but the entire body of findings describes a municipal water-supply connection process (E-File, councillor certificate, municipal pipe network, 271 wells, APWD) — the stated experts and department do not match the service and process actually discussed.
No departmental processing timeline (in days) is given for water-connection applications, unlike other AN services in this set.
No deemed-approval provision and no validity/renewal requirement are specified for water connections.
Whether the applicant must visit an office in person at any stage (versus everything being handled via E-File) is not explicitly stated.
Use of roughly 271 public wells as a supplementary water source during low-availability periods is flagged as a practice worth replicating elsewhere.
No risk-based classification or specific redundant-requirement review is described for this service.
